title: Effect of Surface Area on Rate
content:
# Effect of Surface Area on Rate

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Describe how surface area affects reaction rate
- Explain the effect using collision theory
- Design experiments to investigate surface area effects
- Give examples of surface area effects in everyday life

## Introduction

When a solid reacts with a liquid or gas, only the particles on the **surface** of the solid can collide with the other reactant. Increasing the surface area exposes more particles and speeds up the reaction.

## Key Concepts

### The Effect

**Increasing surface area increases the rate of reaction.**

- Smaller pieces = larger total surface area
- More surface particles can react
- Faster reaction

### Visualizing Surface Area

[DIAGRAM: Large cube vs same cube cut into smaller pieces showing increased total surface area]

**Example:**
- 1 cube with 2 cm sides: surface area = 6 × 4 = 24 cm²
- Cut into 8 cubes with 1 cm sides: surface area = 8 × 6 × 1 = 48 cm²
- Same total volume, but double the surface area

### Collision Theory Explanation

**Why does surface area affect rate?**

1. In a solid, only particles on the **surface** are exposed
2. Only surface particles can collide with liquid/gas reactant particles
3. Smaller pieces have more total surface area
4. More surface particles are available to react
5. More collisions can occur per second
6. More successful collisions per second
7. Rate increases

[DIAGRAM: Large lump with few collision points vs powder with many collision points]

### Comparing Forms

| Form | Surface area | Rate |
|------|--------------|------|
| Large lump | Small | Slow |
| Small pieces | Medium | Medium |
| Powder | Large | Fast |

**Examples:**
- Marble chips vs marble powder in acid
- Iron filings vs iron nails in acid
- Sugar cubes vs granulated sugar dissolving

### Effect on Graphs

```
Volume of gas (cm³)
    ↑
    |          Powder ___________
    |         /
    |       /   Small pieces ___________
    |     /    /
    |   /    /   Large pieces ___________
    | /    /    /
    |/___/____/________________________→
                    Time (s)
```

**Key observations:**
- Powder (largest surface area) → steepest curve
- All reach **same final volume** (same mass of solid)
- Total amount of product is the same
- Only the rate is different

### Investigating Surface Area

**Reaction:** Calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid
$$\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{2HCl} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$$

**Variables:**
- Independent: Surface area (form of calcium carbonate)
- Dependent: Volume of CO₂ produced / Time taken
- Control: Mass of CaCO₃, concentration and volume of acid, temperature

**Method:**
1. Measure 50 cm³ of 1M HCl into flask
2. Connect to gas syringe
3. Add 5 g of large marble chips
4. Record volume of gas every 30 seconds
5. Repeat with small chips and powder (same mass)
6. Plot all results on same axes

**Important:** Use the same **mass** of solid, not the same number of pieces.

### Safety Considerations

**Powders can be dangerous:**
- Very fine powders can form explosive mixtures with air
- Flour dust, coal dust, metal powders can explode
- This is because of the extremely large surface area
- Dust explosions in mills and mines are a real hazard

**In the lab:**
- Don't create dust clouds
- Work in well-ventilated areas
- Keep powders away from flames

### Everyday Examples

**Cooking:**
- Diced vegetables cook faster than whole ones
- Minced meat cooks faster than steak
- Grated cheese melts faster than sliced

**Fires:**
- Kindling (small sticks) catches fire easier than logs
- Sawdust burns rapidly
- Metal filings burn; metal blocks don't

**Medicine:**
- Powder medicines dissolve faster than tablets
- Chewing tablets increases surface area

**Digestion:**
- Chewing food increases surface area
- Allows enzymes to work faster

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** Explain why powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster with acid than marble chips.

**Solution:**
- Powdered calcium carbonate has a much larger surface area than marble chips of the same mass
- More calcium carbonate particles are exposed on the surface
- More particles can be hit by acid particles
- There are more collisions per second between CaCO₃ and HCl
- This means more successful collisions per second
- Therefore the rate of reaction is faster

---

**Example 2:** A student investigates the reaction of magnesium with acid using ribbon, turnings, and powder. Sketch the expected graphs on the same axes.

**Solution:**
```
Volume of H₂ (cm³)
    ↑
    |          Powder ___________
    |         /
    |       /   Turnings ___________
    |     /    /
    |   /    /   Ribbon ___________
    | /    /    /
    |/___/____/________________________→
                    Time (s)
```

All three lines reach the same final volume because the same mass of magnesium is used. Powder is steepest (fastest rate), ribbon is least steep (slowest rate).

---

**Example 3:** Explain why flour mills have to be very careful about dust explosions.

**Solution:**
- Flour is a powder with very high surface area
- When flour dust is suspended in air, huge surface area is exposed to oxygen
- A small spark can provide activation energy
- The flour reacts (burns) extremely rapidly with oxygen
- This causes an explosion due to rapid gas expansion
- Mills use strict safety measures to prevent dust accumulation

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Using different masses of solid when comparing surface areas
- **Correct:** Use the same mass - this keeps amount of reactant constant

- **Mistake:** Thinking more surface area produces more product
- **Correct:** Surface area affects rate, not total amount of product

- **Mistake:** Forgetting that only surface particles can react
- **Correct:** This is the key concept - particles inside the solid can't collide

## Practice Questions

1. Explain, using collision theory, why increasing surface area increases reaction rate. (4 marks)

2. A student reacts 2 g of calcium carbonate with excess acid in three forms: lump, chips, and powder. Sketch the volume vs time graphs. (3 marks)

3. Why do the three graphs in question 2 all reach the same final volume? (2 marks)

4. Describe an experiment to investigate how surface area affects the rate of reaction between marble and hydrochloric acid. Include variables and method. (6 marks)

5. Explain why:
   a) Diced potatoes cook faster than whole potatoes (2 marks)
   b) Coal dust can cause explosions in mines (2 marks)

6. Why is it important to use the same mass of solid when investigating surface area? (2 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Surface area | The total area of the exposed outer surface |
| Powder | A solid in very small particles (large surface area) |
| Dust explosion | Rapid combustion of fine particles suspended in air |
| Exposed particles | Particles on the surface that can collide with other reactants |

## Summary

- **Larger surface area = faster reaction**
- Only **surface particles** can collide with reactants
- Smaller pieces = more surface area = more particles exposed
- More collisions → more successful collisions → faster rate
- Same mass produces same total product (just faster or slower)
- **Graphs:** Powder steepest, lumps least steep, all reach same final value
- **Safety:** Fine powders can cause dust explosions
- **Control variables:** Same mass, same acid concentration and volume, same temperature
